title: The 3 Stanford Tools That Rewired How We Think In 19 Minutes
summary: Part two of the sisters' series on the most important tools from Stanford GSB and HBS, covering three decision frameworks: Jobs to be Done (people hire products for emotional jobs), decision trees with expected value (list options, map outcomes, assign probability and payoff, multiply), and OKRs applied to personal life. Each comes with company examples from LinkedIn, Netflix, Amazon and Sisters Matcha plus a mini exercise for listeners.

ideas.idea: People do not buy products, they hire them to do a job, and that job is usually emotional rather than purely functional.
ideas.detail: The Jobs to be Done framework, created by Clay Christensen at HBS, is one of the most misunderstood ideas in product and marketing; at LinkedIn, Cherie's team asked whether people update their profile for visibility, validation or to get hired, because the answer determines what to build.

ideas.idea: Customers often hire a product for the narrative and community around it, not just its quality.
ideas.detail: Jean says buyers of Sisters Matcha are partly purchasing the story of the small family farm in Wazuka, Japan that both sisters worked on and the documented journey of how it is made.

ideas.idea: Apply Jobs to be Done to yourself: be honest about what people hire you for at work, whether competence, confidence, calm in a storm or personality.
ideas.detail: The first mini exercise asks listeners to name the job their role or service actually performs for others and post it in the comments.

ideas.idea: Make big decisions with a four-step decision tree: list options, sketch outcomes, assign probabilities and payoffs, and multiply to get expected value.
ideas.detail: The framework forces clarity when stakes are high and combines qualitative and quantitative thinking; it is how to make important life decisions without losing your mind.

ideas.idea: A job offer that looks amazing on paper can be a 'meh' offer once you weight best, worst and most likely scenarios by probability.
ideas.detail: Jean mapped three outcomes for an impressive offer, assigned values and likelihoods, and found the expected value underwhelming; by contrast entrepreneurship looks risky and low-value early on but has huge option value and upside when mapped the same way.

ideas.idea: Billion-dollar companies use expected value rather than gut instinct, and you can borrow the same math for personal decisions.
ideas.detail: Netflix uses it to greenlight shows, VC firms to pick investments, and Amazon for pricing models; 'gut instinct is cute, but billion-dollar companies use math'.

ideas.idea: Staying stuck is worse than being wrong; a decision framework lets you be wrong safely with the most informed choice available.
ideas.detail: People delay decisions from fear of looking wrong. Cherie cites LinkedIn head of product Tomer Cohen's saying 'I may be wrong, but I'm not confused', which Jean adapts to 'I may be wrong, but I have clarity'.

ideas.idea: Get a decision out of your head and onto paper; the model does not have to be perfect to beat the swirl.
ideas.detail: Mini exercise: pick a decision living rent-free in your brain, map two to three outcomes with values and probabilities, multiply, and compare expected values.

ideas.idea: Run your life like a product roadmap using OKRs, with an objective and numeric key results that measure it.
ideas.detail: OKRs were invented by Andy Grove at Intel, popularized by Google and Stanford's design program, and used at nearly every tech company; a personal example is objective 'get in better shape' with key results like gym three days a week for five weeks or hit 20% body fat.

ideas.idea: Sharing personal OKRs with your work team creates social accountability and lets colleagues support your goals.
ideas.detail: Both sisters' teams at LinkedIn and elsewhere shared personal OKRs like learning piano or dancing; teammates would tell someone to leave for their gym class because they knew it was that person's OKR, and everyone rushed to hit goals before the quarterly review.

ideas.idea: The most valuable part of OKRs is the exercise of figuring out which key results actually ladder up to the objective.
ideas.detail: Breaking a scary goal into actionable milestones makes it less intimidating and forces you to think about what you must really do to achieve the outcome.

ideas.idea: OKRs are a guardrail against urgency: if a request does not ladder up to your stated OKRs, you can decline it.
ideas.detail: Without OKRs everything feels urgent and you tackle things as they come; with them you can say 'I'd love to, but I have to focus on XYZ first', a valid excuse that everyone has visibility into. It is disastrous when your OKRs do not ladder up to your org's OKRs, a topic for their Power and Influence episode.

ideas.idea: A personal OKR for mental health could be three therapy sessions, journaling twice a week and one full rest day per quarter.
ideas.detail: Jean's example for the mini exercise, which Cherie says she will borrow.

ideas.idea: Together the three frameworks answer three questions: are you solving the right problem, how to stop spiraling and decide, and what to prioritize.
ideas.detail: Jobs to be Done checks the problem, decision trees end the spiral, and OKRs prioritize what matters; the sisters urge listeners to actually do the exercises rather than nod along.
